extracted.intended_audience: marketers, salespeople, negotiators, communicators, and others seeking to craft ethically persuasive requests
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing requests, marketing messages, and interpersonal appeals using Dr. Robert Cialdini's empirically supported principles of persuasion. Focuses on practical, often low-cost tactics that increase compliance ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply put, people are obliged to give back to others the form of a behavior, gift, or service that they have received first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be the first to give; ensure what you give is personalized and unexpected. Restaurant studies: giving a single mint at the end of a meal typically increased tips by around 3%; two mints increased tips about 14% (quadrupling), and giving one mint then pausing and offering an "extra mint" increased tips by 23%—showing that how the gift is given matters. Use unexpected, personalized favors or gifts to trigger reciprocity in ethical ways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scarcity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply put, people want more of those things they can have less of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight uniqueness and what people stand to lose by not acting. Example: British Airways' announcement of ending Concorde service produced a surge in sales despite no change in product or price—scarcity itself raised desire. Effective messages point out what is unique about the proposition and the losses or missed opportunities avoided by acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority
rubrics_metrics.description: People follow the lead of credible, knowledgeable experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signal credibility before making the influence attempt (e.g., diplomas on the wall, uniforms, expert introductions). You generally should not self-praise; instead arrange for third-party introductions that communicate expertise—even if the introducer benefits. Example: real estate offices that had reception staff mention colleagues' credentials saw a 20% rise in appointments and a 15% increase in signed contracts. Simple, visible cues to expertise increase compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: People like to be consistent with the things they have previously said or done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek voluntary, active, public, and ideally written small initial commitments that can scale to larger consistent behaviors. Example: a small postcard in a window signaling support for 'Drive Safely' produced a 400% increase in willingness to erect a larger (unsightly) sign later. Another study reduced missed health appointments by 18% by asking patients, not staff, to write appointment details on the card. Use incremental commitments that build consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liking
rubrics_metrics.description: People prefer to say yes to those that they like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foster similarity, give genuine compliments, and cooperate toward shared goals. In online negotiation studies, groups instructed to exchange personal information and identify similarities reached agreement at ~90% (versus ~55% for 'get down to business' groups), and agreements were typically worth ~18% more to both parties. Look for authentic similarity and sincere compliments before requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially when they are uncertain, people will look to the actions and behaviors of others to determine their own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to what similar others are doing—use honest data about peers' behavior. Hotel towel studies: a message stressing environmental benefits produced ~35% compliance; explicitly stating that ~75% of guests reuse towels increased reuse by ~26%; furthermore, changing wording to point to what comparable previous guests did (e.g., '75% of guests who have stayed in this room reuse their towel') produced as much as a 33% increase. Use descriptive norms about similar others for greater effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity (listed as a universal shortcut) — the sense of shared identity or belonging that increases willingness to comply with requests made by those with whom one feels 'one-ness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page lists Unity as a principle but does not elaborate further here (note: a footnote indicates the 7th principle was added after the original piece). In practice, Unity signals can be built by emphasizing family, tribe, shared values, or group membership to increase compliance; the page does not provide concrete examples or metrics for Unity.
